1.pericope_label: The lot of the half tribe of Manasseh: Machir and the six families

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain the double inheritance from the firstborn clause and unpick the absolute construction of 'to Machir'.

Wesley distinguishes Ephraim's prominence from Manasseh's right of primogeniture and reads Machir for the whole tribe; Clarke holds the man himself long dead and reads the verse of his descendants, well fitted to defend a frontier.
Henry reports Bishop Patrick's concessive rendering, suggests Machir's reputation may date from the quarrel with the men of Gath, and matches the six families against the census list.
Gill marks the western half as those who had no part in Gilead and Bashan.

debates.question: Is 'for Machir' the man or his house?

sides.position: his children, since Machir would now be nearly two hundred years old
Machir himself, named for the whole tribe descended from him

debates.question: How can Manasseh be called the firstborn when Jacob preferred Ephraim?

sides.position: the preference did not touch the right of primogeniture, which carried the double portion
render it concessively — though he was the firstborn

3.pericope_label: The daughters of Zelophehad claim their inheritance; the ten portions

schools.summary: Gill traces the descent that grounds the claim and prefers the plain division of Hepher's portion among the five daughters over the Talmudic reckoning; Calvin refuses every proposed solution to the number and says the data are not there to settle it.
Keil and Delitzsch summarise the petition granted under Moses and repeated before the dividers, and note it was fulfilled at once.
Henry praises the women for pleading their own cause and Joshua for not objecting that they had not served in the wars.

Wesley gives the simplest arithmetic — five portions for the sons, five for the daughters — and insists the sex was no bar; Clarke follows Calmet to the same total and glosses 'portions' as cords, evidence the land was measured with a line.

debates.question: How do ten portions fall to six sons and five daughters?

sides.position: five for the surviving sons and five for the daughters, Hepher and Zelophehad drawing none
six for the families and four for the daughters, on account of father, grandfather and childless uncle
holders: Jarchi and Kimchi from the Talmud (as reported by Gill)

sides.position: the number of families is unrecoverable, so the sum cannot be checked; only that equity was observed

outliers.note: Says expositors either disguise the difficulty or trifle with it, and that four portions for five daughters is simply absurd.

7.pericope_label: The borders of Manasseh, interlocking with Ephraim

schools.summary: Henry gives the shape of the territory sea to Jordan and reads the interlocking with Ephraim as designed, to keep up correspondence between the tribes.
Gill warns that 'from Asher' means a town of that name, not the tribe, and places the river Kanah against Ephraim's border.
Keil and Delitzsch note this southern boundary coincides with Ephraim's northern one, given here with greater precision.

Clarke renders Kanah as the valley of the reeds and works out the junction with Asher at the sea, allowing that towns were held inside other tribes' limits; Wesley explains the meeting by necks of land jutting past Zebulun.

debates.question: How did Manasseh and Ephraim 'meet together in Asher on the north'?

sides.position: Asher reached to Carmel and Manasseh to Dor, so the two joined at the Mediterranean
necks of land belonging to Ephraim and Manasseh jutted out past Zebulun to touch Asher's border

schools.summary: Gill gathers the later history of Beth-shean from Josephus, the Maccabees and the Talmud; Calvin cannot account for cities held inside other tribes' lots and reads the grant as an inheritance held in hope rather than possession.

Clarke derives Scythopolis from the Cuthites and places Dor and En-dor; Wesley explains the transfer of towns between unequal portions and offers 'the third part of that country' for 'three countries'.

debates.question: Whence the name Scythopolis for Beth-shean?

sides.position: from Succoth nearby, not from the Scythians
from the Cuthites planted in the Samaritan cities by the kings of Assyria

debates.question: How could towns be granted in Asher and Issachar before those lots were settled?

sides.position: the narrative anticipates, relating what had not yet taken place
portions were adjusted between tribes when one proved too narrow and another too large

outliers.note: Passes on the Talmudic saying that if the garden of Eden were in the land of Israel, Beth-shean was the gate of it.

12.pericope_label: The Canaanites not driven out, but put to tribute

schools.summary: Gill leaves the failure between weakness and sloth without forcing a choice; Calvin refuses both excuses and calls the tribute a worse fault than the delay.
Clarke charges them with neither grace nor courage, and reports the alternative rendering that they could not resolve to destroy the cities and the Canaanites consented to stay.
Keil and Delitzsch state the sequence plainly: unable to exterminate, they made them tributary when they grew stronger, and still did not drive them out.
Henry says they served their own ends by conniving, and may have learned the practice from Ephraim.

debates.question: Why were the Canaanites not driven out?

sides.position: they had not the strength at first, or were negligent and lost the advantage
they had neither grace nor courage, and preferred profit to obedience
read the Hebrew as 'could not resolve to destroy' — a negotiated coexistence

outliers.note: Observes that those on whom tribute is imposed are thereby taken under one's faith and protection — the opposite of the commission Israel had.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch deny any real ground for the complaint and answer it from the second census figures.
Gill asks who is speaking and concludes Ephraim at least countenanced the request; Calvin judges the complaint factually true but dishonestly used, since it counted unconquered ground as nothing.
Wesley supplies the occasion and offers two senses of 'one portion'.
Henry suspects they hoped for favour from a judge of their own tribe, and praises Joshua's impartiality as an example to all in public trusts.

debates.question: Did the house of Joseph really receive only one lot?

sides.position: yes, and by design, so that brothers of one father should be neighbours — with limits set by numbers, so no injustice followed
either one lot afterwards divided by arbitrators, or a portion barely enough for one of the two
the complaint had no real ground at all, on the census figures

outliers.note: Notes they were thankful for the increase God had given without presuming on its continuance — blessed me hitherto.

schools.summary: Gill sums the reply as retorting their own argument upon them.
Wesley turns the retort into a charge to act and identifies the Perizzites and giants as forest and cave dwellers; Clarke stresses that Joshua granted a licence to clear, not a change in the lot.
Keil and Delitzsch explain what clearing the wood would mean and locate mount Ephraim as a limestone range from Kirjath-jearim to the plain of Jezreel.
Henry presses the answer into a rule about idleness: would they dig, they need not beg.
Gill gives two senses of 'the hill is not enough' — insufficient, or unobtainable; Calvin treats the whole speech as quibbling to avoid a reasonable suggestion.
Wesley reads the objection as anticipating the rejoinder about the valleys and describes the chariots as armed with scythes and swords; Clarke identifies the hill as Gilboa.
Henry says the chariots mowed men down like corn, and states the grievance at its strongest: a good portion in bad hands.
Keil and Delitzsch map the land of the valley as the Jordan plain near Beisan together with the plain of Jezreel, the Esdraelon of later writers.

debates.question: What does 'the hill is not enough for us' mean?

sides.position: the highland will not suffice even when won and cleared
the hill cannot be obtained by us at all, the Perizzites and giants holding the woods

outliers.note: Finds the appeal to iron chariots the worst of it, since they had already seen the Lord trample horses and chariots without difficulty.

17.pericope_label: Joshua repeats the answer with its reasons: thou shalt drive them out

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the repetition as answering cowardice, and take the mountain and its outgoings to be the wooded hills and their bordering plains.
Gill notes both tribes were present and that Manasseh needed the enlargement most, more of its cities being still in Canaanite hands.

Wesley makes the promise conditional on endeavour; Clarke turns it into strategy — hold the heights and the defiles and the valleys follow — and closes with three reflections on discontent, firmness and sloth.
Henry applies it inward: we straiten ourselves by imagining the difficulties greater than they are.

outliers.note: Ends the chapter on the reader rather than on Israel: God will not reverse his purpose to accommodate our idleness.
